title: Sensor Placement
subtitle: Where the signal is measured changes what can be inferred
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating sensor placement within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain sensor placement without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in sensor placement.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to sensor placement.

sections.explainSimply: Electrodes are placed using standard scalp landmarks so recordings can be repeated and communicated.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: A scalp site captures a mixture of sources shaped by reference, volume conduction and artifact. Site labels are not one-to-one labels for underlying cortical functions.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Placement should follow a reproducible system, with laterality, reference, ground and montage documented. Training rationales should avoid simplistic “site equals trait” claims.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Trying to tune a faint radio station: contact, interference and antenna placement determine what reaches the speaker.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand sensor placement to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Moving a sensor a few centimetres can change signal and artifact exposure.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using sensor placement predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Moving a sensor a few centimetres can change signal and artifact exposure. Evidence classification: established acquisition standard.
